title: One global clock domain for the cores and on-chip L2, with skew treated as a budgeted resource
where_in_paper: Clock distribution section (a 'Clock distribution' / 'Clocking' topic area, later in the paper)
decision: Distribute a single global clock across the chip so that the two processor cores and the on-chip L2 operate synchronously at the same frequency, with clock skew budgeted and controlled in the distribution network, rather than bridging separately clocked islands with synchronizers or locally generated clocks.
rationale: My recollection of the thrust of the argument: the core-to-L2 bandwidth is so high that synchronizer latency and clock-crossing uncertainty could not be afforded, and a single domain makes the entire chip timeable against one cycle; skew is then an engineering budget managed by balancing/tuning the distribution network.
outcome: The paper reports hardware that ran at/near its target frequency with measured skew within budget; I cannot recall specific ps or GHz figures stated here.
weakest_point: The network topology detail (balanced tree vs. grid, tuned segments, 'local clock buffers') is general IBM/POWER4 practice, not something I can tie to this paper's text; and if the paper instead emphasizes multiple clock domains (e.g. L2 or the fabric interface at a divided frequency), my 'single domain' direction is reversed. I am only ~70% confident cores and L2 ran at the same frequency.

title: Full-chip static-timing sign-off with unit-level timing budgets / interface contracts
where_in_paper: Timing methodology (design methodology / chip integration and timing-closure discussion)
decision: Close timing using static timing analysis at the full-chip level, with each macro/unit carrying timing budgets or boundary timing contracts (arrival/required-time assertions) that could be renegotiated between units as the design converged, rather than signing off on the basis of simulated critical paths.
rationale: As far as I can recall the thrust: simulation of a design this large cannot cover the path space, whereas STA gives complete coverage and explicit budgets let units be designed and closed somewhat independently and then integrated.
outcome: The paper reports the flow converged to tape-out and that first hardware met its frequency target; no quantitative closure results recalled.
weakest_point: Whether tool names (e.g. IBM's EinsTimer) or the phrase 'timing assertions' actually appear here, and whether the paper frames this as a weighed decision at all — it may simply describe the flow. Very likely I am reconstructing a rationale the paper states differently.

title: Power distribution, IR drop and power density treated as first-class physical-design constraints
where_in_paper: Power distribution / power and thermal topic area (possibly overlapping packaging-module discussion)
decision: Design the on-chip power grid and its module/package connection against explicit IR-drop and current-density limits, i.e. treat power delivery and power density as design constraints during physical design rather than as a post-layout verification check.
rationale: Recollection of thrust only: at this power level supply noise directly consumes timing margin and electromigration/current density bound the grid, so the grid had to be designed to a drop budget up front.
outcome: The paper reports a very high chip power/dissipation figure (I believe in the ~100–120 W class) with measured drop within budget; I cannot recall the numbers as stated in this paper.
weakest_point: Whether power/IR-drop has its own section in THIS paper or is mostly in the packaging/module companion material; the ~115 W number is general POWER4 knowledge and may not be stated here at all.

title: 0.18 μm bulk CMOS with copper interconnect as the technology base for the design
where_in_paper: Technology / process description (early section of the paper)
decision: Implement the chip in IBM's 0.18 μm-class bulk CMOS with copper wiring and multiple metal levels (I do not recall the count), and size the wiring resource accordingly for a >1 GHz two-processor chip. I do not recall this being presented as a weighed choice with named rejected options.
rationale: Recollection of thrust: copper's lower resistance (and improved current-carrying capability) was what made the global wiring and power delivery feasible at this frequency and density — but I may be supplying this reasoning myself rather than recalling the paper's.
outcome: The paper reports a very large transistor count (POWER4 is commonly cited at ~174 M transistors) on a single die; I cannot reliably recall the die size as given here.
weakest_point: Everything quantitative: process name/generation, number of metal levels, whether low-k dielectric was used (I believe it was not at POWER4), and the die area (~267 mm²?) are all uncertain and drawn from general POWER4 knowledge rather than the paper text.

title: Two out-of-order cores plus shared on-chip L2, off-chip L3 and fabric bus
where_in_paper: This belongs to the companion 'POWER4 system microarchitecture' paper (same issue, pp. 5–25), not to this circuit/physical-design paper — included only to mark the boundary
decision: Integrate two processor cores with a shared multi-banked on-chip L2 (with multiple L2 controllers) and an off-chip L3/fabric interface; the physical-design paper would only inherit this as a floorplanning input.
rationale: This is microarchitecture rationale (throughput per chip, shared-L2 bandwidth), i.e. the companion paper's territory — I flag it rather than presenting it as content of this paper.
outcome: Not reported as an outcome in this paper.
weakest_point: I cannot rule out that this paper's floorplan/integration section restates the core/L2 floorplan, in which case a floorplan-level version of it IS legitimately here — but the organizational description itself is the companion paper's.
